Chandrika had taught at the Ramgarh government school for two years when she decided to open an evening reading corner in the empty panchayat room. The night before the gram sabha, she sat under the lantern and wrote three lines in her notebook: Children here have no books at home. I loved reading when I was small. I will be proud of this even if only two children come.
At the meeting, she explained the plan. The sarpanch, Lokesh-ji, scratched his head. "Who will lock the room?" Nobody clapped. One uncle asked about the electricity bill.
Chandrika felt the old sting in her chest, the wish for someone to say well done. Then she remembered the notebook. She answered about the lock and the bill, and walked home calm.
On Monday, five children came.

qa.a: Five children came on Monday.

qa.a: She felt a sting of disappointment and the wish for someone to say well done, but the notebook lines helped her stay calm.

The offer came on a Thursday in Porto: team lead, more money, Saturdays at the office. Priscila had sung in the neighbourhood choir every Saturday for six years.
Before she called anyone, she sat at the kitchen table and wrote on the back of an envelope: What do I want to be proud of in five years? She wrote: the choir, my evenings, not being tired all the time. Then: Would I still choose this if no one said "good decision"?

My roommate Vaibhav came back from the chemistry lab at seven, dropped his bag and announced, "My willpower is finished for today. Fully used up." Then he opened a packet of chips and skipped the run we'd planned.
I didn't say anything, but I'm a psychology student, so I noticed. Last month our professor spent a whole lecture on this exact idea, that self-control is like a fuel tank that drains. She showed us that very large repeat studies, run in many labs, found the effect much weaker than first claimed, or not at all. She also mentioned studies where people who believed willpower runs out seemed to give up sooner.
Was Vaibhav really drained? Maybe. The lab was four hours long. Or maybe he just believes the tank story. I honestly can't tell from outside. I just ate a few of his chips and kept my mouth shut.

qa.q: How long was Vaibhav's chemistry lab?
qa.a: The lab was four hours long.

qa.q: How does the narrator feel watching Vaibhav claim his willpower is used up?
qa.a: The narrator feels doubtful and curious, remembering the lecture on failed replications, but also unsure, because Vaibhav might really be tired.

qa.q: What could the narrator gently suggest to Vaibhav next time?
qa.a: The narrator could suggest a short walk instead of the full run, treating the tiredness as real while not assuming a fixed tank of willpower has run dry.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see his evening?
qa.a: To Vaibhav it feels obvious that his willpower is gone after four hours in the lab, so skipping the run seems fair and natural to him.

grounding: It shows a psychology student observing a friend blame a drained willpower tank while knowing large replications failed to confirm strong depletion effects.

Before: In first year, Parveen's intro textbook had a neat diagram of willpower as a battery. It made sense. She drew it in her notes with a lightning bolt.
During: In a third-year methods seminar, three weeks later into the term, the professor put up the results of large multi-lab repeat studies. The strong depletion effect mostly vanished. "Tiredness is real," the professor said. "Low motivation is real. But the battery? We don't know." Parveen crossed out her old lightning bolt and wrote a question mark.
After: On Saturday her friend Tushar lay on the hostel bed. "Can't go to the gym. Spent all my willpower on the assignment."
Parveen almost nodded. Then she said, "Maybe you're tired. Or maybe you're telling yourself you're empty. Want to try just ten minutes and see?" Tushar groaned but sat up. She wasn't sure she was right either.

"Ira, you're studying psychology now, so let me tell you about my hostel days. I'm your Kalyani Mami, the one who argued with every professor.
In my third year, everyone believed willpower was a tank. Use it up on exams, and it's gone. My hostel-mate Rukmini swore by it. After every paper she'd say, 'Tank empty,' and eat a whole box of sweets.
Then our research methods teacher showed us something that stayed with me. Bigger studies, done again and again in many places, did not find the strong effect. Some found that what you believe about your tiredness changes how tired you act.
I watched Rukmini that week after exams. Was she truly spent, or did the belief do half the work? I could never be sure. What I did learn was to be careful before calling anything proven."

qa.a: She said, "Tank empty," and ate a whole box of sweets.

qa.q: What choice did young Kalyani make after that class?
qa.a: She chose to be careful before calling anything proven, holding the tank idea as uncertain rather than a fact.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt if someone questioned her empty tank?
qa.a: Rukmini might have felt defensive or annoyed, since the tank idea explained her tiredness and made the box of sweets feel deserved.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a psychology student learning that large replications failed to confirm strong depletion and observing a friend's tiredness with uncertainty.

Anand was the agriculture extension officer for six villages around Sirsi, and for months his monthly reports were late. He blamed himself: lazy, careless, bad with paper.
In April he noticed something. By two in the afternoon, after the field visits in the heat, he could barely read a form. At dawn, with the crows and the cool air, his head was sharp.

"Me," Anand said. "Report's done. Go back to sleep."

Olga translated legal contracts from Polish into English, and for a year she had fought her own brain. She would start the hardest documents after lunch, stare at the same clause for an hour and call herself weak.
Then she kept a small log for two weeks. Between eight and eleven, she translated twice as many pages with fewer mistakes. After three, she mostly reread the same lines.
Now her day in Kraków has a shape. Contracts from eight to eleven, door closed. Emails and invoices after lunch. Sunday afternoon she cooks soup for four days and writes the week's meals on the fridge.

Olga smiled. "I stopped trying to beat my afternoon self."
